title: Friction on Ramps
short: Find the angle where a block starts to slip, tan θ = μ_s, and its acceleration once it slides.
trouble: Students point friction down the slope for a block that is sliding down.

blocks.html: Put together Inclined Planes and Static Friction, and a ramp becomes a friction meter. Tilt a board slowly with a block on it: at first static friction holds it, then at one particular angle it lets go.

A block starts to slip when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$. Once sliding down, kinetic friction points up the slope: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$. Sliding up, both gravity's part and friction point down the slope: the deceleration is $g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

Along the slope, gravity pulls with $mg\sin\theta$; static friction can resist with at most $\mu_s F_N = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$. The block holds while $mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, that is, while $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$. The mass cancels, so a heavy block and a light one of the same material slip at the same angle. Friction always opposes sliding (or the sliding that would happen), so its direction flips when the motion does.

blocks.name: ph-dynamics

opts.task: Tilt the ramp slowly. Note the angle where the block slips, and check it against tan θ = μ_s.

blocks.cap: With μ_s = 0.5 the block holds until tan θ = 0.5, at θ ≈ 26.6°; then it slides with kinetic friction.

blocks.title: The slipping angle
blocks.q: A block sits on a board with $\mu_s = 0.6$. At what angle does it slip?

blocks.title: Sliding down
blocks.q: A block slides down a $35^\circ$ ramp with $\mu_k = 0.2$. Find its acceleration.
steps: Friction points up the slope, against the sliding.

blocks.title: Shoved up the slope
blocks.q: The same block is shoved up the same ramp. While it slides up, what is its deceleration?
steps: Now gravity's part and friction both point down the slope.
$$a = 9.8(0.574 + 0.164) \approx 7.23\ \text{m/s}^2,$$ so it stops quickly, then slides back down at $4.02\ \text{m/s}^2$.

blocks.html: Pointing friction down the slope for a block that is sliding down. Friction resists the sliding, so it points up the slope. Check: for a block sliding down, its acceleration must be smaller than the frictionless $g\sin\theta$; if your answer is bigger, friction has the wrong sign.
Try it in the Science Lab: Forces at Work.
